question: In crashes with motorcyclists, what do drivers often say afterward?
choice_a: That the motorcyclist waved them through
choice_b: That the motorcycle was traveling far too slowly
choice_c: That they never saw the motorcycle
choice_d: That the motorcycle had no headlight at all
explanation: In crashes with motorcyclists, drivers often say that they never saw the motorcycle -- a motorcycle's outline is much smaller than a car's, and most drivers are not looking for motorcycles.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.19, 'Increasing Conspicuity'

question: The manual suggests adopting what mindset to increase awareness of your surroundings?
choice_a: Focus only on the vehicle directly ahead
choice_b: Assume every driver has already seen you clearly
choice_c: Assume drivers will always yield the right-of-way
choice_d: Pretend you're invisible to other motorists
explanation: A good strategy is to pretend you're invisible. If you assume other motorists can't see you, you'll tend to ride in a hyper-aware mindset and notice more details in your surroundings.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.19, 'Increasing Conspicuity'

question: Even if a driver does see a motorcycle approaching, why might the rider still not be safe?
choice_a: Smaller vehicles appear farther away than they actually are, so drivers often pull out thinking they have plenty of time
choice_b: Drivers are legally required to yield only to cars, not motorcycles
choice_c: Motorcycles are invisible in daylight regardless of clothing
choice_d: This scenario never actually causes crashes
explanation: Even if a driver does see you coming, you aren't necessarily safe -- smaller vehicles appear farther away than they actually are, and it's common for drivers to pull out in front of motorcyclists thinking they have plenty of time, and too often they are wrong.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.19, 'Increasing Conspicuity'

question: Since a rider's body makes up about half of the visible surface area of the rider/motorcycle unit, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Wearing all-black gear for a professional look
choice_b: Wearing bright-colored clothing to increase the chance of being seen
choice_c: Riding only at night to reduce visibility concerns
choice_d: Removing reflective material, since it distracts other drivers
explanation: Most crashes occur during daylight hours. Wear bright-colored clothing to increase your chances of being seen -- your body is half of the visible surface area of the rider/motorcycle unit.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.19-20, 'Clothing'

question: Which jacket/vest colors does the manual list as best bets for being seen?
choice_c: Bright orange, red, yellow, or green
explanation: Bright orange, red, yellow, or green jackets/vests are your best bets for being seen; any bright color is better than drab or dark colors.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.20, 'Clothing'

question: Where does the manual say reflective material is especially useful for helping drivers spot a rider from the side?
choice_a: Reflective material is not recommended anywhere on rider gear
choice_d: On a vest and on the sides of the helmet
explanation: Reflective material on a vest and on the sides of the helmet will help drivers coming from the side to spot you; it can also help drivers both ahead and behind.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.20, 'Clothing'

question: During the day, a motorcycle with its headlight on is how much more likely to be noticed compared with one without?
choice_c: Only slightly more likely, by about 5%
explanation: Studies show that, during the day, a motorcycle with its headlight on is twice as likely to be noticed. Use low beam at night and in fog.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.20, 'Headlight'

question: The manual notes that Minnesota law requires a motorcycle's headlight to be on:
explanation: The operator must have the headlight on at all times when riding in Minnesota.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.IV, 'Motorcycle Operating Rules'

question: Why does the manual recommend using turn signals even when you think no one else is around, or even when your intended move seems obvious?
choice_a: Turn signals are required only above 45 mph
choice_b: It is only a suggestion with no real safety value
choice_c: Signal lights make you easier to spot and reduce confusion and frustration for surrounding traffic
choice_d: It only matters for group rides, not solo riding
explanation: Use signals anytime you plan to change lanes or turn, even when you think no one else is around and even when what you plan to do seems obvious -- your signal lights make you easier to spot and reduce confusion and frustration for traffic around you.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.20, 'Signals'

question: After completing a turn, why should a rider make sure the turn signal is switched off?
choice_a: It is only a cosmetic issue, not a safety one
choice_b: It has no effect on other drivers' behavior
choice_c: Leaving it on saves the battery
choice_d: A driver may pull directly into the rider's path, thinking the rider plans to turn again
explanation: Once you turn, make sure your signal is off, or a driver may pull directly into your path, thinking you plan to turn again.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.21, 'Signals'

question: The manual recommends flashing the brake light before slowing in which of these situations?
choice_a: When you slow more quickly than others might expect, such as turning off a high-speed highway
choice_b: Only when coming to a complete stop at a red light
choice_d: Flashing the brake light is never recommended
explanation: Help others notice you by flashing your brake light before you slow down, especially when you slow more quickly than others might expect (such as turning off a high-speed highway) or where others may not expect it, like the middle of a block.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.20-21, 'Brake Light'

question: Most motorcycle mirrors are rounded (convex). What effect does this have on judging distance?
choice_a: They make cars seem closer than they actually are
choice_b: They provide a wider view but make cars seem farther away than they actually are
choice_c: They provide no distortion at all compared to flat mirrors
choice_d: They only work properly at night
explanation: Most motorcycles have rounded (convex) mirrors, which provide a wider view of the road behind than flat mirrors but also make cars seem farther away than they actually are; practice with them until you become a good judge of distance.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.21, 'Using Your Mirrors'

question: Why is checking mirrors alone not enough before changing lanes?
choice_a: Mirrors only show what's directly behind, never to the sides at all
choice_b: Mirrors are unreliable and should never be used
choice_c: Motorcycles have blind spots like cars, so a head check is also needed
choice_d: It is enough, and a head check is unnecessary
explanation: Checking your mirrors is not enough. Motorcycles have blind spots like cars -- before you change lanes, turn your head and look to the side for other vehicles.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.21-22, 'Head Checks'

question: The manual suggests giving a quick beep of the horn before passing anyone who may move into your lane, such as:
choice_a: Only vehicles displaying a student-driver sign
choice_b: Any vehicle traveling below the speed limit
choice_d: A parked car with someone in the driver's seat, or a pedestrian or bicyclist in the street
explanation: It is a good idea to give a quick beep before passing anyone that may move into your lane, such as a parked car with someone in the driver's seat, or someone riding a bicycle or walking in the street.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.22, 'Horn'

question: At night, why should a rider not let their total stopping distance exceed the distance illuminated by their headlight beam?
choice_a: So the rider can stop within the distance they can actually see
choice_b: It only matters for the low beam, never the high beam
choice_c: It is a legal requirement with no safety basis
choice_d: It has no bearing on stopping ability at night
explanation: Headlight: do not let your total stopping distance exceed the distance your light beam illuminates. Slow down so you can stop within the distance you can see.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.23, 'Riding at Night'

question: Why does the manual say distances are harder to judge at night?
choice_a: Speedometers become less accurate after dark
choice_b: Eyes rely on shadows and light contrasts, which are harder to interpret in darkness
choice_c: Motorcycle headlights are dimmer than car headlights by law
choice_d: Night riding is prohibited, so this scenario never applies
explanation: At night, distances are harder to judge -- your eyes rely upon shadows and light contrasts to determine how far away an object is and how fast it is coming, so open up a three-second or more following distance.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.23, 'Riding at Night'
